query: A TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy has been reported in a single-phase BCC, dendritic state, with a yield strength of about 800 MPa and roughly 40% strain under lower-temperature testing, but at 1273 K it retains only 330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength at 30% strain. For its use as an intermediate layer that transfers heat between W and CuCrZr while preserving structural integrity, what single intervention could overcome this loss of strength at elevated temperature? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the reported baseline, define the applicable thermal and mechanical boundary conditions, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Modifying the processing route to form a refined microstructure with nanometer‐scale, thermally stable oxide precipitates (e.g. TiO) will mitigate the high-temperature strength loss in the TiVNbTa single-phase BCC alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy in its as-cast, single-phase dendritic BCC state with a yield strength of about 800 MPa at lower temperatures and degraded strength at 1273 K.
generation.intervention: Adopt mechanical alloying combined with spark plasma sintering (SPS) with controlled low-level oxygen doping to trigger the in situ formation of nanoscale TiO precipitates and grain refinement.
generation.conditions: The modified alloy is intended for use as an intermediate layer under thermal cycling between ambient and elevated temperatures around 1273 K, and under compressive/tensile loading similar to the reported tests (e.g., 30% strain compressive tests).
generation.structural_mediator: The nano-precipitates (TiO) embedded in a refined BCC matrix that result from the altered processing method.
generation.mechanism: The introduced oxide precipitates act as stable obstacles to dislocation motion at high temperature, while the refined grain structure increases grain boundary area for strengthening. Together, these effects reduce high-temperature softening and help maintain higher yield and compressive strengths.
generation.predicted_outcome: At 1273 K, the modified alloy is expected to retain a substantially higher yield strength and compressive strength relative to the baseline (330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength), though the exact improvement magnitude is uncertain; a beneficial improvement (on the order of 30-50% strength retention increase) is hypothesized.
generation.baseline: As reported, the as-cast TiVNbTa alloy exhibits ~800 MPa yield strength at lower temperatures and degrades to 330 MPa yield strength (and 423 MPa compressive strength) at 1273 K.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for intermediate layers operating between tungsten and CuCrZr, where high-temperature (up to ~1273 K) structural integrity under moderate plastic strains (around 30-40%) is required.
generation.uncertainty: The degree of improvement in high-temperature mechanical properties is uncertain due to possible trade-offs (e.g. changes in ductility or sensitivity to oxygen-induced embrittlement) and differences in alloy composition and processing response relative to similar high-entropy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of TiVNbTa alloys: one using the conventional melting route resulting in the dendritic single-phase BCC microstructure, and the other using mechanical alloying combined with spark plasma sintering with a controlled oxygen addition aimed at precipitating TiO nanophases. Subject both sets to high-temperature testing at 1273 K under identical tensile and compressive loading conditions. Microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM) should confirm the presence and distribution of the nano-oxide precipitates in the processed samples.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain size, precipitate size, and distribution via TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanically alloyed and SPS-processed alloy with controlled oxygen doping does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature yield and compressive strength (e.g., less than a 30% increase compared with the baseline) or if adverse microstructural effects (e.g. excessive embrittlement) dominate, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The alloy has moderate strength at RT, with a yield strength of ∼647 MPa, a tensile strength of 680 MPa and an elongation of 15 %, i.e. it has no advantages over typical medium- and high-entropy alloys. However, its strength does not significantly decrease at medium and high temperatures, remaining at 405 MPa at 800 °C. This indicates the advantage of a weak dependence of strength on temperature. Fig. 4 shows the fracture surface of ht-TiVNb after tension. Shear plastic deformation and cavity-aggregated dimples appear after applying tension at RT. Tensile fracture at 600 °C is characterised by plastic deformation near the grain boundaries and trans-granular quasi-cleavage within the grains, accompanied by oxidation. Fracture at 800 °C shows an intergranular fracturing mode with notable high-density slip lines and traces of tearing, indicating strong intragranular bonding forces. The fracture surface is covered with an oxide layer, indicating that the alloy is susceptible to oxygen-induced intergranular embrittlement at this temperature. Besides, ht-TiVNb is resistant to cracking. After 80 % compression strain at 800 °C, multiple cracks developed in the am-TiVNb surface (Fig. 6a and b). This phenomenon was greatly inhibited in ht-TiVNb, such that only a single crack was observed (Fig. 6c). We speculate that the improvement of cracking resistance of ht-TiVNb is due to its coarsened grain size (up to the millimeter scale), which largely reduced its GB (grain boundary) area while increasing its thermal conductivity. High-entropy alloys and Ti (22 W/m K at RT) have low thermal conductivities []. The thermal conductivity of Ti-containing high-entropy alloys, such as AlCr1.5CuFeNi2Tix, is lower (only 11–14 W/m K at RT); this value decreases with increasing Ti content []. Therefore, during compression, am-TiVNb with μm-scale grain size has a large stress concentration. The coarse-grained ht-TiVNb alloy exhibited improved resistance to stress concentration, improving its resistance to cracking. In summary, although the strength of the TiVNb alloys at RT is not high, they show weak temperature dependence of strength and their ductility is superior to those of most reported lightweight high-entropy alloys. Equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi refractory HEA has been successfully synthesized by MA and SPS. It exhibits excellent mechanical properties with compressive yield strength of 2709 MPa, fracture strength of 3115 MPa and fracture strain of 11.4%. The sintered alloy consists of a BCC matrix phase, a minor BCC phase, and an FCC precipitated phase, identified as TiO. The average grain size of BCC matrix phase and TiO are measured to be 1.35 μm and 0.46 μm, respectively. Compared with the as-cast NbMoTaWVTi alloy, the compressive yield strength and fracture strength of the alloy in this work are extraordinarily elevated, while the ductility is slightly reduced. Thus, mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering is a promising way to further improve mechanical properties of the refractory HEA by means of grain refinement and precipitation strengthening.
